newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss army to help guard world Zionist anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Swiss army to help guard world Zionist anniversary.

text.p: The Swiss army will be called in to back up local police guarding an international gathering of Jewish leaders in the Swiss city of Basle in August, the government said on Wednesday.

The cabinet agreed to deploy about 730 soldiers to help secure August 31 celebrations marking the 100th anniversary of the first Zionist congress, whose Basle meeting launched a movement that led to the founding of Israel in 1948.
The armed recruits would be under police command during the security mission from August 20 to September 1, when some 1,500 guests from Israel and around the world are expected.
"It is in Switzerland's domestic and foreign interests to make sure the ceremonies are carried out in a dignified way," defence minister Adolf Ogi told reporters.

The event is due to include Israeli Knesset (parliament) speaker Dan Tichon standing in for Israeli President Ezer Weizman, who cancelled his appearance in January due to what officials said were scheduling conflicts.

The ceremonies will commemorate the first congress of the Zionist movement for a Jewish state started by Theodor Herzl in Basle, the country's second biggest city and situated on the Franch and German borders.
Ogi's Department of Military Affairs, or defence ministry, said the troops could be reinforced vy up to several hundred additional men if Basle authorities request more forces.

"The army's job will be to relieve police of secondary duties such as guarding buildings, directing traffic or controlling the airport. Outside the meeting building you will hardly see any soldiers, just police," a ministry spokesman said.
The troops will include an airforce detachment called into provide helicopters for the police, the spokesman said.

Switzerland's militia army, which every adult male is required to serve in, is occasionally called on to help guard big international meetings such as the Geneva summit of U.S. and Russian presidents Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev in 1985.
Federal Police chief Urs von Daeniken was quoted as saying Middle East tensions could give rise to threats to the Zionist commemoration.
But far-right militants in Switzerland could also pose a danger, he said, according to the Swsis news agency SDA.
